pos: n. (Johannes Polyander a Kerckhoven, 1568–1646, professor of theology at Leiden and delegate to the Synod of Dort)
etymology: Greek polyandros, of many men, populous; a grecised form of the surname Van den Kerckhoven, of the churchyard.
biblical_def: Johannes Polyander was called to the chair of theology at Leiden in 1611, in the middle of the Arminian crisis, as the man who could be set beside Episcopius without the faculty exploding. He was a Netherlander raised in exile at Metz, pastor of the Walloon congregation at Dordrecht before his call, moderate in temper and entirely firm in doctrine — the combination the university needed and had not had. He sat in the Synod of Dort, served on the committee that drafted the canons, and afterwards shared in the new translation of the Dutch Bible authorised by the synod. His most lasting work came in 1625, when he and three colleagues produced the Synopsis of a Purer Theology, fifty-two disputations covering the whole body of divinity, which taught Reformed students across Europe for a century. He is the example of a particular kind of churchman: not the most brilliant man in the room and the one the room could agree to listen to. “Let all things be done decently and in order” (1Co 14:40).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines synopsis as a general view, a collective view of the parts of a science, and disputation as a formal argument in a school.
webster_full: SYNOP'SIS, n. A general view, or a collection of things or parts so arranged as to exhibit the whole or the principal parts in a general view.
DISPUTA'TION, n. The act of disputing; a reasoning or argumentation in opposition to something; an exercise in colleges.
PROFES'SOR, n. One that publicly teaches any science or branch of learning; particularly, an officer in a university.
CAN'ON, n. In ecclesiastical affairs, a law or rule of doctrine or discipline enacted by a council.
scriptures: Let all things be done decently and in order.
Act 15:6
And the apostles and elders came together for to consider of this matter.
Eph 1:11
In whom also we have obtained an inheritance, being predestinated according to the purpose of him who worketh all things after the counsel of his own will:
Tit 1:9
Holding fast the faithful word as he hath been taught, that he may be able by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers.
corruption_summary: The Leiden professor the faculty could agree to hear, and the Synopsis of a Purer Theology.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the assumption that moderation of temper implies softness of doctrine, so that a man who does not quarrel must be a man who will trade. Polyander answers it. He held the Reformed doctrine of grace without a hair's deviation and sat at Dort on the drafting committee, and he did it while remaining the colleague whom the other side could still speak to.

The principle to recover is that the assembling of the church to settle a question is itself a scriptural institution with a scriptural manner. “And the apostles and elders came together for to consider of this matter” (Act 15:6) establishes the council; “Let all things be done decently and in order” (1Co 14:40) governs how it proceeds. Both verses are necessary. A synod with the doctrine and without the order is a riot, and a synod with the order and without the doctrine is a committee.

pos: n. (Antonius Thysius, 1565–1640, professor at Harderwijk and Leiden, co-author of the Synopsis)
etymology: Latin Antonius, a Roman family name; Thysius, a latinised form of the Dutch surname Thys.
biblical_def: Antonius Thysius taught first at Harderwijk and from 1619 at Leiden, where he joined Polyander, Walaeus and Rivet in the four-man faculty that rebuilt the university's theology after Dort. He had studied at Leiden and Geneva, had been a pastor, and brought to the chair the habit of a man who has had to explain the doctrine to people rather than merely defend it to colleagues. His share of the Synopsis of a Purer Theology is the plainest written of the four. The Synopsis itself deserves its reputation: fifty-two disputations, each a compact treatment of one locus, the whole thing readable in a way that later scholastic manuals are not, and shaped throughout by the decisions of the synod that had just closed. The four professors divided it among themselves and each defended his own portion publicly, which is why the book has the texture of argument rather than lecture. “Study to shew thyself approved unto God, a workman that needeth not to be ashamed” (2Ti 2:15).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines locus as a place, and theology as divinity, the science of God and divine things.
webster_full: THEOL'OGY, n. Divinity; the science of God and divine things; the science which teaches the existence, character and attributes of God.
PROFES'SOR, n. One that publicly teaches any science or branch of learning.
FAC'ULTY, n. The body of persons to whom are committed the instruction and government of a college.
MAN'UAL, n. A small book, such as may be carried in the hand; a book of instruction.
scriptures: Study to shew thyself approved unto God, a workman that needeth not to be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of truth.
And the things that thou hast heard of me among many witnesses, the same commit thou to faithful men, who shall be able to teach others also.
Tit 1:9
Holding fast the faithful word as he hath been taught, that he may be able by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers.
Till I come, give attendance to reading, to exhortation, to doctrine.
corruption_summary: One of the four Leiden professors who wrote the Synopsis and defended each his own part.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the modern separation of the seminary from the pulpit, which produces teachers who have never had to explain a doctrine to a farmer and pastors who have never had to defend one to a critic. The Leiden four had done both, and the Synopsis shows it: the disputations are compact because the men writing them knew how long a reader's patience lasts.

The principle to recover is that theological teaching is a trust handed on under a double requirement — the man must have it, and he must be able to give it. “And the things that thou hast heard of me among many witnesses, the same commit thou to faithful men, who shall be able to teach others also” (2Ti 2:2). Four links are in that verse: Paul, Timothy, faithful men, and others. A faculty is simply the third link organised. “Study to shew thyself approved unto God” (2Ti 2:15) is the labour that keeps the chain from breaking.

pos: n. (Sibrandus Lubbertus, c. 1555–1625, professor at Franeker and chief opponent of Arminius)
etymology: Frisian Sibrand, from Old Germanic, victory-sword; Lubbertus, a latinised form of Lubbert, people-bright.
biblical_def: Sibrandus Lubbertus was a Frisian who studied at Wittenberg, Geneva under Beza, and Basel, and came home to be the first professor of theology at the new university of Franeker, where he taught for forty years. He was the most persistent of Arminius's opponents and began sounding the alarm years before most of the Dutch church would take it seriously, writing to England and to the German Reformed to say that the Leiden chair was teaching a doctrine of grace that could not be reconciled with the Belgic Confession. He was called difficult, and he was; he quarrelled with Vorstius, with Grotius, and with several men on his own side. But he was right about the thing he would not drop, and his persistence is a large part of why the States-General finally called a national synod at all. Being tiresome in a good cause is not a virtue. Being unwilling to let a false doctrine pass into a church's teaching because objecting is socially costly is one. “ye should earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints” (Jud 1:3).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines contend as to strive in debate, to dispute earnestly, and pertinacious as holding or adhering firmly to any opinion.
webster_full: CONTEND', v. To strive in debate; to dispute earnestly; to contest.
PERTINA'CIOUS, a. Holding or adhering to any opinion, purpose or design, with obstinacy; stubborn.
UNIVER'SITY, n. An assemblage of colleges established in any place, with professors for instructing students.
PROTEST', v. To affirm with solemnity; to make a solemn declaration against.
scriptures: Jud 1:3

Beloved, when I gave all diligence to write unto you of the common salvation, it was needful for me to write unto you, and exhort you that ye should earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints.
Gal 1:8
But though we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel unto you than that which we have preached unto you, let him be accursed.
For I know this, that after my departing shall grievous wolves enter in among you, not sparing the flock.
Also of your own selves shall men arise, speaking perverse things, to draw away disciples after them.
corruption_summary: Franeker's first theologian, who would not let the Arminian doctrine pass in silence.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the preference for peace over precision that treats the man who raises the alarm as the cause of the trouble. Lubbertus was raising his objections from about 1604 and was told for more than a decade that he was exaggerating, importing foreign quarrels, and disturbing a church that was managing. He was not exaggerating. The Remonstrance of 1610 said in public what he had said was being taught in private.

The principle to recover is that Paul expected the danger to come from inside and said so to the elders he had trained. “Also of your own selves shall men arise, speaking perverse things, to draw away disciples after them” (Act 20:30). The watchman who names it will be unpopular with his own, which is the position Jude writes into: “it was needful for me to write unto you, and exhort you that ye should earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints” (Jud 1:3). Needful, not congenial.

pos: n. (Festus Hommius, 1576–1642, scribe of the Synod of Dort)
etymology: Latin Festus, festal, joyful; Hommius, a latinised form of the Frisian surname Homme.
biblical_def: Festus Hommius was a Frisian pastor at Leiden who served as one of the two scribes of the Synod of Dort and afterwards as regent of the States College there. The synod sat for a hundred and eighty sessions over seven months with delegates from eight foreign churches, and somebody had to keep the record in Latin while it happened. Hommius did, and the acts of Dort are his as much as anyone's. He had prepared for it: before the synod he published a catalogue setting the Remonstrant positions side by side with the Belgic Confession and the Heidelberg Catechism, article against article, so that the delegates arrived knowing exactly what was in dispute. He later shared in the great Dutch Bible translation the synod ordered. His career is the administrative spine of the Reformed settlement in the Netherlands, and it is exactly the work that disappears from the histories. “It seemed good to me also, having had perfect understanding of all things from the very first, to write unto thee in order” (Luk 1:3).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines scribe as a writer, a notary, one who registers, and acts as the records of a court or assembly.
webster_full: SCRIBE, n. A writer; a notary; one who registers or records; an official writer.
ACTS, n. plural. The records of transactions, as the Acts of an assembly or council.
REG'ISTER, n. A written account or entry of acts, judgments or proceedings.
CAT'ALOGUE, n. A list or enumeration of the names of men or things disposed in a certain order.
scriptures: Luk 1:3
It seemed good to me also, having had perfect understanding of all things from the very first, to write unto thee in order, most excellent Theophilus,
Luk 1:4
That thou mightest know the certainty of those things, wherein thou hast been instructed.

Then pleased it the apostles and elders, with the whole church, to send chosen men of their own company to Antioch with Paul and Barnabas; namely, Judas surnamed Barsabas, and Silas, chief men among the brethren:
Act 16:4
And as they went through the cities, they delivered them the decrees for to keep, that were ordained of the apostles and elders which were at Jerusalem.
corruption_summary: The scribe of Dort, who kept the record of a hundred and eighty sessions.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the idea that a council's authority rests on the eminence of the men who sat in it, with the consequence that the record of what they actually decided is a secondary matter. It is the reverse. A synod binds by what it published, and the published acts are the whole of what it left behind. Where the record is thin or partisan, the decision degenerates within a generation into a party slogan.

The principle to recover is the one Luke states for his own writing and the apostles practise at Jerusalem: a decision is useless until it is written down and carried to the churches. “And as they went through the cities, they delivered them the decrees for to keep, that were ordained of the apostles and elders which were at Jerusalem” (Act 16:4). That verse has a scribe behind it. Luke names the purpose of careful writing exactly: “That thou mightest know the certainty of those things, wherein thou hast been instructed” (Luk 1:4).

pos: n. (Jacobus Trigland, 1583–1654, Amsterdam pastor, Leiden professor and historian of the Arminian controversy)
etymology: Latin Jacobus, from Hebrew Yaaqob, a supplanter; Dutch Trigland, from a place-name, faithful land.
biblical_def: Jacobus Trigland was pastor at Amsterdam through the worst of the Arminian struggle and afterwards professor at Leiden for twenty years. He was a controversialist by necessity and a historian by choice, and the second is what he is worth remembering for. His Ecclesiastical Histories of 1650 is a documentary account of the whole Remonstrant controversy from its beginning, written against Uytenbogaert's rival version, and it works by printing the documents. Where the Remonstrant history characterised, Trigland quoted. That is a method with a theology behind it: if the case is true, the papers will carry it, and a reader given the papers does not need to be told what to conclude. He also sat on the committee for the Dutch Bible translation. His weakness was the common one of the party historian — he selects, and the reader must know he is reading an advocate. His strength is that he gives you the means to check him. “These were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so” (Act 17:11).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines history as a narration of facts and events arranged in order, and document as a written instrument conveying information or proof.
webster_full: HIS'TORY, n. An account of facts, particularly of facts respecting nations or states; a narration of events in the order in which they happened.
DOC'UMENT, n. Written instruction, evidence or proof; any official or authoritative paper containing instructions or proof.
CONTROVER'SIALIST, n. One who carries on a controversy; a disputant.
AD'VOCATE, n. One who pleads the cause of another in a court; one who defends or vindicates.
scriptures: These were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so.
He that is first in his own cause seemeth just; but his neighbour cometh and searcheth him.
Joh 5:39
Search the scriptures; for in them ye think ye have eternal life: and they are they which testify of me.
Isa 8:20
To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them.
corruption_summary: The historian of the Arminian controversy, who argued by printing the documents.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the writing of church history as characterisation: the other side is summarised, in the historian's own words, and the reader is never given anything to check. Both parties in the Dutch quarrel did it, and Trigland's answer to Uytenbogaert was to print the papers and let a reader compare. He was still an advocate and the selection is his; but a selection a reader can see is a different thing from a paraphrase he cannot.

The principle to recover is Luke's commendation of the Bereans, which is a commendation of verification and not of credulity. “These were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so” (Act 17:11). Readiness of mind and daily searching, together. Solomon states the forensic half of the same rule: “He that is first in his own cause seemeth just; but his neighbour cometh and searcheth him” (Pro 18:17).

pos: n. (George Carleton, 1559–1628, bishop of Llandaff and Chichester, head of the British delegation to Dort)
etymology: Greek Georgios, a husbandman; English Carleton, from a place-name, the free peasants' settlement.
biblical_def: George Carleton led the four-man British delegation that King James sent to the Synod of Dort, and his presence there is one of the better-attested facts about the doctrine of the English church before the Laudian turn. He was bishop of Llandaff, a Calvinist of settled conviction, and he and his colleagues voted with the synod against the Remonstrants on every head of doctrine. The delegation differed from the Dutch on one practical point — they argued for a more guarded statement on the extent of the atonement — and the canons as adopted left room for their language. Carleton also made a nuisance of himself defending episcopacy when a Dutch speaker disparaged it, which tells you he was not there as anyone's instrument. He wrote afterwards a defence of the synod against English critics. The plain fact his career establishes is that in 1618 the Church of England sent bishops to a Reformed synod to condemn Arminianism, and they went willingly. “whom he did predestinate, them he also called” (Rom 8:30).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines delegate as a person appointed and sent by another with powers to transact business, and episcopacy as the government of the church by bishops.
webster_full: DEL'EGATE, n. A person appointed and sent by another with powers to transact business as his representative.
EPIS'COPACY, n. The government of the church by bishops; that form of ecclesiastical government in which diocesan bishops are established.
SYN'OD, n. A council or meeting of ecclesiastics to consult on matters of religion.
DEP'UTY, n. One appointed or deputed to act for another; a substitute in office.
scriptures: Rom 8:30
Moreover whom he did predestinate, them he also called: and whom he called, them he also justified: and whom he justified, them he also glorified.
Rom 8:29
For whom he did foreknow, he also did predestinate to be conformed to the image of his Son, that he might be the firstborn among many brethren.
Eph 1:4
According as he hath chosen us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and without blame before him in love:
It seemed good unto us, being assembled with one accord, to send chosen men unto you with our beloved Barnabas and Paul,
corruption_summary: The English bishop who led King James's delegation to Dort and voted against the Remonstrants.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is a reading of English church history that treats Reformed doctrine as a Puritan deviation from an Anglican mean. Carleton is the inconvenient fact. He was a bishop, he was sent by the king, he defended episcopal government in the synod itself against a Dutch critic, and on every point of the doctrine of grace he voted with Dort. The English delegation signed the canons.

The principle to recover is the golden chain, which is the plainest statement in Scripture that salvation is one continuous act of God from first to last. “Moreover whom he did predestinate, them he also called: and whom he called, them he also justified: and whom he justified, them he also glorified” (Rom 8:30). Four links and no leakage between them. The ground of the whole is set outside time and outside us: “he hath chosen us in him before the foundation of the world” (Eph 1:4).

pos: n. (Walter Balcanquhall, 1586–1645, Scottish delegate to the Synod of Dort)
etymology: Germanic Walter, ruler of the army; Scots Balcanquhall, from a place-name in Fife.
biblical_def: Walter Balcanquhall was the son of an Edinburgh minister who had stood up to King James, and he was sent to Dort in 1618 as the Scottish member of the British delegation. He was young for it, in his early thirties, and his letters home to Sir Dudley Carleton are among the best eyewitness sources for what the synod was actually like from day to day — who spoke, how long, what the foreign delegates thought of each other, where the real disagreements lay. He signed the canons. His later career went the other way: he became a dean, attached himself closely to Charles I and to Laud, and is generally held to have had a hand in the Scottish service book of 1637 that set off the riot in St Giles' and the Covenant after it. The Covenanters hated him and he died in exile with the royalists. That a man who voted at Dort should end as an agent of the Laudian policy is not a contradiction to be smoothed over; it is a warning about the distance between subscribing a sound canon and keeping a sound course. Paul puts the warning where the confidence is: “let him that thinketh he standeth take heed lest he fall” (1Co 10:12).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines dean as an ecclesiastical dignitary in cathedral churches, and liturgy as a form of prayers and ceremonies used in public worship.
webster_full: DE'AN, n. In England, an ecclesiastical dignitary in cathedral and collegiate churches, the head of a chapter.
LIT'URGY, n. In a general sense, all public ceremonies that belong to divine service; a formulary of public devotions.
SUBSCRIP'TION, n. The act of subscribing or writing one's name underneath; attestation by signature.
COV'ENANT, n. A mutual consent or agreement of two or more persons, to do or to forbear some act.
scriptures: Wherefore let him that thinketh he standeth take heed lest he fall.
Watch ye, stand fast in the faith, quit you like men, be strong.
Let us hold fast the profession of our faith without wavering; (for he is faithful that promised;)
Rom 8:30
Moreover whom he did predestinate, them he also called: and whom he called, them he also justified: and whom he justified, them he also glorified.
corruption_summary: The Scot who signed the canons of Dort and ended as an agent of the Laudian policy.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the use of a man's signature on a good document as a permanent certificate of his soundness. Balcanquhall signed the canons of Dort at thirty-two and spent his forties helping to force a service book on the Church of Scotland. Nothing in the record suggests he renounced what he signed; he simply came under other influences, took other preferments, and let the practical direction of his life be set by a court.

The principle to recover is that subscription is not perseverance and that Scripture warns the confident man specifically. “Wherefore let him that thinketh he standeth take heed lest he fall” (1Co 10:12) is addressed to people with every outward advantage. Paul's four imperatives are all present-tense and continuous: “Watch ye, stand fast in the faith, quit you like men, be strong” (1Co 16:13). And the profession is to be held “without wavering” (Heb 10:23), which assumes the wavering is possible.

pos: n. (John Hales of Eton, 1584–1656, English scholar and chaplain at the Synod of Dort)
etymology: Hebrew Yochanan, the LORD is gracious; English Hales, from Old English halh, a nook or recess of land.
biblical_def: John Hales went to Dort in 1618 as chaplain to the English ambassador and sent home a series of letters that remain the liveliest account of the synod in English. He is remembered chiefly for a remark he is said to have made during Episcopius's defence, that he there bade John Calvin good night — a sentence usually reported as the moment an honest witness saw the Reformed case collapse. The story will not bear that weight. The remark comes to us at second hand, from a friend's memoir written long afterwards, and Hales's own letters from the synod show no such turn; what they show is a scholar increasingly weary of dogmatic certainty on all sides. He became in later life a byword for learned, charitable latitude, and that is the real drift to name. His settled position was that the points on which Christians must agree are very few and the rest may be held loosely. It is a position the Reformed must refuse, and refuse plainly, because Scripture does not treat its doctrine as a short list with a wide margin. “All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine” (2Ti 3:16).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines latitude as extent, freedom from restraint, laxity, and fundamental as pertaining to the foundation, essential.

scriptures: All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness:
Jud 1:3

Beloved, when I gave all diligence to write unto you of the common salvation, it was needful for me to write unto you, and exhort you that ye should earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints.
For I have not shunned to declare unto you all the counsel of God.
Hold fast the form of sound words, which thou hast heard of me, in faith and love which is in Christ Jesus.
corruption_summary: The Dort chaplain of the famous remark, and the latitude that actually marked his life.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Two corruptions run together here. The first is the anecdote. A second-hand sentence from a memoir written decades later is regularly cited as though Hales had published a recantation at the synod, and his own contemporary letters do not support it. The second is the position he genuinely came to hold, which is the one that matters: that the necessary articles are few, the rest are opinion, and peace is bought by shrinking the list.

The principle to recover is that Scripture nowhere divides its teaching into a small binding core and a large indifferent remainder. “All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine” (2Ti 3:16) — all of it, and profitable for that purpose. Paul's account of his own ministry is the same claim from the preacher's side: “For I have not shunned to declare unto you all the counsel of God” (Act 20:27). A ministry that shortens the list has shunned something.

pos: n. (Matthias Martinius, 1572–1630, rector of the Bremen gymnasium and delegate to the Synod of Dort)
etymology: Greek Matthias, from Hebrew Mattithyahu, gift of the LORD; Martinius, a latinised form of Martin.
biblical_def: Matthias Martinius came to Dort as one of the three delegates from Bremen and gave the synod its most interesting internal difficulty. He was Reformed, he rejected the Remonstrant doctrine, and he voted for the canons. He also held a view of the covenant and of the death of Christ that did not fit the prevailing Dutch formulation: he wanted to say that Christ's death is in some genuine sense offered for all men, with the saving intention particular to the elect. Gomarus challenged him to a formal disputation on the floor of the synod and the moderator had to stop it. The canons as finally drawn were framed to include men like Martinius without endorsing his distinctive formulation. That is a fact worth holding onto. Dort was not a narrowing of the Reformed faith to one school; it was a boundary drawn against the Remonstrance, broad enough inside to contain Bremen and Britain as well as Franeker and Leiden. Martinius was besides a Hebraist and the author of a serious Latin etymological dictionary. “All that the Father giveth me shall come to me; and him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out” (Joh 6:37).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines atonement as expiation, satisfaction made for an offence, and intention as design, purpose, the fixed direction of the mind.
webster_full: ATO'NEMENT, n. Expiation; satisfaction or reparation made by giving an equivalent for an injury.
INTEN'TION, n. Design; purpose; the fixed direction of the mind to a particular object.
EXTENT', n. Space or degree to which a thing is extended; compass; bulk; size.
GYMNA'SIUM, n. A school; a place where the youth are instructed.
scriptures: Joh 6:37
All that the Father giveth me shall come to me; and him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.
My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me:
And I give unto them eternal life; and they shall never perish, neither shall any man pluck them out of my hand.
Eph 1:4
According as he hath chosen us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and without blame before him in love:
corruption_summary: The Bremen delegate the canons were framed to include, and the disputation the moderator stopped.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse comes from both directions. Some use Martinius to argue that Dort was hopelessly divided and its canons therefore mean little; others write him out and present the synod as a single school imposing a single formula. Neither is honest. The synod had a real internal range on the extent of the atonement and drew its canons to hold that range while shutting out the Remonstrance, which is what a confessional boundary is for.

The principle to recover is that the particularity of salvation is stated in Scripture as a matter of the Father's giving and the Son's keeping, and that this is where the weight falls rather than on a calculation of quantity. “All that the Father giveth me shall come to me; and him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out” (Joh 6:37). The Shepherd then says what becomes of them: “I give unto them eternal life; and they shall never perish, neither shall any man pluck them out of my hand” (Joh 10:28).

pos: n. (Abraham Scultetus, 1566–1624, Palatinate court preacher and delegate to the Synod of Dort)
etymology: Hebrew Abraham, father of a multitude; Latin Scultetus, a latinised form of Schultheiss, a village magistrate.
biblical_def: Abraham Scultetus was a Silesian who became professor at Heidelberg and court preacher to the Elector Palatine, and he came to Dort in 1618 as one of the Palatinate delegates. He preached the sermon at the synod's opening. His theology was straightforward Heidelberg Calvinism and he was a capable historian of the Reformation's first century. His judgment in politics was catastrophic. He went with Frederick V to Prague in 1619 when that prince accepted the crown of Bohemia, and there set about stripping the images out of the cathedral of St Vitus in a city of Utraquist and Catholic sentiment that had not asked for it. The offence was enormous, it hardened Bohemia against the new king, and within a year the White Mountain had destroyed the whole enterprise and brought the Palatinate itself under Spanish occupation. Scultetus later wrote with real remorse about his part. The lesson is not that images should have been left; it is that a reformation imposed on a people who have not been taught is not a reformation. “Let all things be done decently and in order” (1Co 14:40).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines iconoclast as a breaker or destroyer of images, and imprudence as want of discretion, indiscretion.
webster_full: ICON'OCLAST, n. A breaker or destroyer of images; one who opposes the worship of images.
IMPRU'DENCE, n. Want of prudence; indiscretion; want of caution or circumspection.
COURT'-PREACHER, n. A preacher attached to the household of a prince or sovereign.
ELECT'OR, n. In the German empire, a prince who had a voice in the election of the emperor.
scriptures: Let all things be done decently and in order.
Let us not therefore judge one another any more: but judge this rather, that no man put a stumblingblock or an occasion to fall in his brother's way.
But take heed lest by any means this liberty of yours become a stumblingblock to them that are weak.
Seest thou a man that is hasty in his words? there is more hope of a fool than of him.
corruption_summary: The Dort delegate who stripped St Vitus' and helped lose Bohemia in a year.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the treatment of Scultetus at Prague as an argument against the second commandment itself — as though the disaster proved that images in worship are a matter of taste after all. It proves nothing of the kind. What it proves is that a true doctrine enforced on a population that has never been taught it produces resentment rather than reformation, and arms the doctrine's enemies with a grievance they will use for a century.

The principle to recover is that the apostles subordinate even the exercise of a genuine liberty to the condition of the people watching. “But take heed lest by any means this liberty of yours become a stumblingblock to them that are weak” (1Co 8:9). Paul applies the same rule to judgment between brethren: “judge this rather, that no man put a stumblingblock or an occasion to fall in his brother's way” (Rom 14:13). Solomon supplies the proverb Scultetus needed in 1619: “Seest thou a man that is hasty in his words?” (Pro 29:20).
